questions.stem: A client with a prior DVT is recovering after total hip arthroplasty. The client reports calf discomfort from the sequential compression device and asks to leave it off. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Remove the compression device for the remainder of the shift and rely on the prescribed anticoagulant because pharmacologic prophylaxis replaces mechanical methods.","B":"Leave the compression device off until the surgeon rounds, keep the client in bed, and avoid ambulation because walking may worsen calf discomfort or reveal an unrecognized thrombus.","C":"Pause the device, assess the leg and skin, correct the fit or application, then resume prescribed prophylaxis and mobilize the client as ordered if no contraindication is found.","D":"Reduce the device pressure below the prescribed setting and use it only while the client sleeps, because partial overnight compression provides equivalent prophylaxis."}}
questions.rationale: A client with prior DVT after total hip arthroplasty remains at elevated VTE risk. Contemporary arthroplasty pathways use multimodal prevention that includes risk-appropriate pharmacologic and mechanical prophylaxis plus early mobilization. Device discomfort should prompt assessment of the limb, skin, fit, and application rather than unilaterally abandoning prescribed prophylaxis. If the device cannot be tolerated safely, the nurse should escalate so the prophylaxis plan can be reassessed.
questions.source_name: AAOS Now — ERAS and risk-stratified VTE prevention after total joint arthroplasty
questions.source_detail: AAOS 2026 ERAS guidance identifies arthroplasty patients as VTE-risk patients and supports pharmacologic plus mechanical prophylaxis according to local policy with early mobilization; contemporary AAOS discussion emphasizes higher risk with prior VTE.

questions.stem: A client preparing for elective abdominal surgery asks to shave the operative area with a razor the night before admission. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"“Shave the area after your antiseptic shower tonight so any small skin irritation has several hours to resolve before the incision is made.”","B":"“Hair should not be removed routinely; if removal is necessary for the procedure, clippers near the time of surgery are preferred to a razor.”","C":"“Use a new razor immediately before coming to the hospital because a clean blade prevents the skin changes associated with surgical-site infection.”","D":"“Remove the hair with a razor after applying antiseptic solution because chemical skin preparation prevents infection from shaving-related abrasions.”"}}
questions.rationale: Routine preoperative shaving is not recommended. Razor shaving can irritate or abrade skin and increase infection risk. CDC surgical-site-infection guidance has long recommended avoiding hair removal unless it interferes with the operation and, when removal is necessary, using clipping rather than shaving close to the procedure according to the surgical protocol.
questions.source_name: CDC — Surgical Site Infection Prevention Guideline and SSI Prevention Basics
questions.source_detail: Current CDC SSI materials advise patients not to shave near the surgical site; CDC SSI prevention recommendations specify avoiding routine hair removal and preferring electric clippers when removal is necessary.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic adult with no previous diabetes diagnosis has a fasting plasma glucose of 145 mg/dL on routine screening. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The single result establishes diabetes immediately because any fasting plasma glucose above 126 mg/dL is diagnostic without additional testing.","B":"The result is in the prediabetes range, so no diagnostic confirmation is needed unless the fasting plasma glucose later exceeds 200 mg/dL.","C":"The result should be treated as normal variation because fasting plasma glucose is not a diagnostic test in adults without classic hyperglycemic symptoms.","D":"The result meets the diabetes threshold, but without unequivocal hyperglycemia a second abnormal test result is required to confirm the diagnosis."}}
questions.rationale: An FPG of 145 mg/dL exceeds the ADA diagnostic threshold of 126 mg/dL. However, in an asymptomatic person without unequivocal hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, ADA 2026 requires confirmatory testing. Confirmation can be a second abnormal result from the same test at another time or another accepted diagnostic test, obtained in a timely manner.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026: Diagnosis and Classification
questions.source_detail: ADA 2026: FPG ≥126 mg/dL meets the diagnostic threshold; in the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results/confirmatory testing.

questions.stem: A hospitalized adult receiving hypotonic fluid has a serum sodium of 128 mmol/L with new headache and confusion. Which action should the nurse anticipate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Treat the value as mild asymptomatic hyponatremia and repeat the sodium with routine morning laboratory testing before changing the plan of care.","B":"Escalate urgently because the client has symptomatic hyponatremia; treatment decisions should be driven by symptoms and may require monitored hypertonic saline.","C":"Delay intervention until the sodium falls below 125 mmol/L because neurologic symptoms at 128 mmol/L are unlikely to be related to hyponatremia.","D":"Administer a large volume of hypotonic IV fluid to raise circulating volume because rapid free-water replacement is the preferred treatment for neurologic symptoms."}}
questions.rationale: A sodium of 128 mmol/L is moderate biochemical hyponatremia, and new headache plus confusion are moderately severe symptoms in Society for Endocrinology guidance. The severity of symptoms may not parallel the absolute sodium value; management decisions should be driven by the clinical presentation. Symptomatic hyponatremia with these neurologic findings warrants urgent escalation and monitored treatment, which may include hypertonic sodium chloride under appropriate clinician supervision.
questions.source_name: Society for Endocrinology — Emergency Management of Severe and Moderately Severely Symptomatic Hyponatraemia
questions.source_detail: 2022 guidance: Na 125–129 mmol/L is moderate biochemical hyponatremia; confusion/headache are moderately severe symptoms; treatment decisions are based on clinical symptoms and symptomatic cases require urgent monitored management.

questions.stem: A nurse has just inserted a small-bore nasogastric feeding tube. The client has no respiratory distress, aspirate was obtained, and an air bolus was heard over the epigastrium. What should the nurse do before the first feeding?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Begin the feeding because aspirate plus epigastric auscultation together provide adequate confirmation of gastric placement before initial tube use in this client.","B":"Obtain radiographic confirmation showing the tube’s course before the first feeding, because bedside findings do not replace initial radiographic verification.","C":"Use external tube length as the deciding check and begin the feeding when the measurement matches the length documented immediately after insertion.","D":"Repeat air-bolus auscultation with another nurse and begin the feeding when both clinicians hear the expected sound over the epigastric area there."}}
questions.rationale: Bedside observations can help predict tube location during insertion, but they do not establish safe initial placement. AACN states that the auscultatory air-bolus method should not be used to determine location and that a blindly inserted feeding tube should be confirmed radiographically, with the entire tube course visualized, before its initial use for feeding or medication administration.
questions.source_name: AACN — Initial and Ongoing Verification of Feeding Tube Placement in Adults
questions.source_detail: AACN Practice Alert: do not use auscultatory air-bolus testing to determine tube location; confirm a blindly inserted feeding tube radiographically before initial feeding or medication use.

questions.stem: A family member is learning passive range-of-motion exercises for a client with severe weakness. During shoulder movement, the family member feels firm resistance and the client reports pain. What should the nurse teach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue through the resistance until the expected range is reached, because brief discomfort during passive movement is necessary to prevent contracture formation.","B":"Use several quick repeated movements through the painful range so the joint loosens, then continue the remaining prescribed exercises at the same session.","C":"Support the joint and move it slowly and gently through the prescribed comfortable range; stop and report new pain or resistance rather than forcing movement.","D":"Ask the client to provide active resistance against each movement, because passive range-of-motion becomes more effective when it also strengthens involved muscles."}}
questions.rationale: Passive ROM is performed by an external force while the client relaxes the joint. Proper technique is slow and gentle; overly strenuous stretching can cause discomfort and reduce cooperation. New pain or firm resistance should not be forced through. The joint should be supported and movement kept within the prescribed comfortable range, with unexpected pain or resistance reported for reassessment.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf / Open RN — Nursing Fundamentals: Mobility
questions.source_detail: Nursing Fundamentals describes passive ROM as externally applied movement and directs that stretching be performed slowly and gently; overly strenuous stretching may cause discomfort.

questions.stem: An alert, cognitively intact client reports postoperative pain of 8/10 while resting calmly with normal heart rate and blood pressure. Which nursing response is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Record the pain as mild because normal vital signs and a calm appearance provide more objective evidence than the client’s numeric rating.","B":"Accept the self-report as the primary pain measure, assess characteristics and function, intervene according to the plan, and reassess the response.","C":"Ask a family member to estimate the pain severity before treating, because observer agreement is needed when the client’s behavior does not match the rating.","D":"Delay analgesic intervention until tachycardia, hypertension, guarding, or facial grimacing confirms that the reported pain is physiologically significant."}}
questions.rationale: Pain is subjective, and when an adult can communicate reliably, the patient's self-report is the gold standard for pain assessment. Normal vital signs or a calm appearance do not invalidate a reported pain score. The nurse should assess the pain more fully, intervene according to the care plan, and reassess the response rather than substituting observer behavior or physiologic measures for self-report.
questions.source_name: AACN — Assessing Pain in Critically Ill Adults
questions.source_detail: AACN Practice Alert: because pain is multidimensional and subjective, patient self-report is the gold standard when the patient can report pain; behavioral tools are alternatives when self-report is not possible.
